entries.meaning: Instruments of many kinds sounded, and the city's joy was beyond description. Everyone prayed for Bharata's arrival: ‘May he come quickly so our eyes obtain their reward.’ In markets, roads, homes, lanes and meeting places, people asked one another how many hours remained until tomorrow's auspicious moment and the fulfilment of their wish by Fate. They pictured Rāma seated with Sītā upon a golden throne. Everyone asked when tomorrow would come and propitiated the obstructive gods. Those gods did not enjoy Ayodhyā's celebration, just as a thief does not enjoy a moonlit night. Summoning Śāradā, the gods repeatedly fell at her feet and pleaded: ‘Mother, behold our great calamity and act today so that Rāma abandons the kingdom and goes to the forest, accomplishing every purpose of the gods.’

Hearing the gods' plea, Sarasvatī stood grieving, like a frosty night over a lotus forest. Seeing her, the gods again entreated: ‘Mother, not the slightest fault is yours. Rāma is beyond astonishment and joy; you know his entire power. Living beings receive happiness and sorrow under the sway of their deeds. Go to Ayodhyā for the gods' welfare.’ After they repeatedly clasped her feet, she left reluctantly, judging the celestial intellect mean. ‘They dwell on high yet act basely and cannot bear another's prosperity.’ Reflecting again upon what must follow and how poets would praise her skill, she came joyfully to Daśaratha's city like an intolerable and sorrowful planetary period. Turning the speech and mind of Kaikeyī's dull-witted maid named Mantharā, she made that chest of infamy her instrument.

Mantharā saw the city decorated and heard lovely auspicious music and congratulations. She asked the people why there was celebration; on hearing of Rāma's anointing, her heart burned. The ill-disposed, socially despised hunchback pondered how that very night she might cause disaster. Like a crooked huntress who sees honey and watches an animal to determine how to seize it, she went lamenting to Bharata's mother. The queen smiled and asked why she looked dejected. Mantharā gave no answer, only sighed, enacted a display of feminine emotion and shed tears. The queen laughed: ‘Your cheeks are greatly swollen; perhaps Lakṣmaṇa has taught you a lesson—that is what I think.’ Still the profoundly malicious maid did not speak, but exhaled darkly like a serpent. Becoming afraid, the queen asked whether Rāma, the king, Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata and Śatrughna were safe. Hearing Bharata's name pained the hunchback's heart.

Mantharā replied, ‘Who could instruct me, Mother? By whose power would I answer back? Who is safe today except Rāma, whom the king makes heir apparent? Fate has become exceedingly favourable to Kauśalyā; beholding her pride, it can no longer stay hidden in her heart. How could you fail to go and see all that splendour whose sight has disturbed my mind? Your son is abroad, yet you have no concern, for you think our husband is under your control. You greatly love sleep and a soft bed and do not perceive the king's cunning.’ Hearing these words and recognizing a tainted mind, the queen rebuked her: ‘Now be quiet, mischief-maker. If you ever speak so again, home-wrecker, I shall seize your tongue and have it pulled out.’ Knowing people with one eye, lameness, a hump or crooked conduct to be devious—and especially a female maid—the mother of Bharata spoke with a smile.

Kaikeyī continued, ‘Sweet-speaker, I have given you this warning, but even in dream I feel no anger toward you. That alone will be the giver of an auspicious day and hour on whichever day your statement proves true. It is the lovely custom of the solar lineage: the eldest is master and the younger brothers his servants. If Rāma's anointing truly takes place tomorrow, friend, ask and I shall give whatever pleases your heart. Kauśalyā and all the others are mothers alike; by his innate nature Rāma is dear to them. He shows particular love toward me—I have tested and seen his affection. If Fate compassionately gives me another birth, may Rāma and Sītā be my son and daughter-in-law. Rāma is dearer to me than life; why does his anointing upset you?’ Swearing by Bharata, she asked Mantharā to speak truth, abandoning deceit and concealment, and explain why she showed distress at a time of joy.

Mantharā replied, ‘All my hopes were fulfilled at once; if I say anything now, I should make myself a second tongue. My unlucky skull deserves to be broken: even sound advice causes you pain. Those who invent falsehoods and make up stories are dear to you, while I am bitter, Mother. From now on I too shall speak only what pleases the mistress; otherwise I shall remain silent day and night. Fate made me deformed and dependent; one reaps what was sown and receives what was given. Whoever becomes king, what harm is it to me? Shall I cease to be a maid and now become a queen? My nature deserves burning only because I cannot bear to see your misfortune. Therefore I merely followed the matter a little; forgive me, goddess—my error is great.’ Hearing the beloved words concealing deep deceit, the weak-minded queen, under the gods' māyā, trusted her enemy as a well-wisher.

Kaikeyī respectfully questioned her again and again, like a Bhīl woman enchanted by a doe's song. Her mind turned exactly as Fate had ordained, and the maid rejoiced as though her trap had caught its mark. Mantharā said, ‘You ask, yet I fear to speak, for I have been branded a home-wrecker.’ She prepared belief in many ways, shaping and cutting her tale; then Ayodhyā's evil planetary period spoke. ‘Rāma says you are dear, and you, queen, say Rāma is dear to you—both statements were formerly true. But those days have passed; when times change, friends become enemies. The sun nourishes the lotus family, yet without water the same sun burns it to ashes. Your co-wife wants to uproot you; dam the excellent water through some means. You feel no concern, trusting in your marital good fortune and believing the king under your control. But the king's mind is tainted though his mouth is sweet, and your nature is straightforward.’

Mantharā continued, ‘Rāma's mother is clever and profound; finding an opening, she has arranged her own affair. The king sent Bharata to his maternal grandparents at Rāma's mother's prompting, as you surely know. All the co-wives serve me well because Bharata's mother is proud of her husband's power; Kauśalyā's grievance against you has not been apparent, Mother, because she is skilled in deceit. She cannot bear the king's special love for you: such is a co-wife's nature. Winning the king to her side, she devised the intrigue and fixed the auspicious hour for Rāma's anointing. The anointing is proper for this lineage, pleases everyone, and seems excellent even to me; but understanding what follows makes me afraid. May Fate give Kauśalyā the very fruit she intends for you.’ Working through crores of crooked devices, Mantharā fabricated this deceptive instruction and told a hundred stories about the co-wife so that hostility would grow.

Under Fate's sway, conviction entered Kaikeyī's heart; the queen again questioned Mantharā and made her swear. Mantharā replied, ‘What shall I ask? You still do not know your own benefit and harm—you are unable to distinguish them, like an animal. The preparations have been underway for a fortnight, yet you learned the news from me only today. Food and clothing are yours by the kingdom; if I tell the truth, the fault is not mine. If I fabricate anything false, may Fate punish me. If Rāma is anointed tomorrow, Fate has sown a seed of calamity for you. Drawing a line, I speak on my strength: lady, you will become a fly in milk. If you serve together with your son, you may remain in the palace; there is no other means. As Kadrū caused suffering to Vinatā, so Kauśalyā will afflict you. Bharata will serve prison, while Lakṣmaṇa will be Rāma's subordinate.’

Hearing these bitter words, Kaikeyī could say nothing; stunned, she withered. Sweat covered her body and she trembled like a plantain tree, while the hunchback pressed teeth upon tongue. Telling crores of deceitful stories, Mantharā urged the queen to keep courage. Kaikeyī's judgment reversed and the mischievous maid became dear; the swan accepted the heron as praiseworthy. ‘Hear, Mantharā, your statement is true: my right eye constantly throbs. Every day and night I see bad dreams but, under the sway of my own affection, did not tell you. What shall I do, friend? My nature is simple; I know neither right hand from left and until today have never deliberately harmed anyone. For what sin has Fate at once given me unbearable suffering?’
